newsitem.title: USA: Probers say more TWA crash evidence unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Probers say more TWA crash evidence unlikely.

text.p: Top investigators into the crash of TWA Flight 800 said on Thursday that with only 5 percent of the plane's wreckage yet to be recovered, there was less likelihood they will find that sabotage downed the jetliner.
"It's just less likely we're going to find the evidence," James Kallstrom, head of the FBI office in New York, told Reuters.

National Transportation Safety Board vice-chairman Robert Francis said on CNN television it was "real disappointing and not normal" to be so far into an air disaster investigation without knowing what caused it.

The Boeing 747 exploded in mid-air and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off New York's Long Island on July 17, just minutes after taking off from Kennedy International Airport on a flight to Paris. All 230 people on board were killed.
In the four months since, investigators have maintained that three theories of the cause -- a bomb, a missile or catastrophic mechanical failure -- have carried equal weight.

"We're not leaning toward anything. We're not changing the odds," Kallstrom said. "And we're not leaving the investigation until we can say it was or wasn't a criminal act. I hope we find the piece that lets us say that."
Asked if investigators may never know the cause, he said, "That's a possibility. But I don't think that will happen."

Francis, asked if he now thought it was less likely that evidence of a bomb or missile would emerge, said, "I think there's some mathematical logic to that, but I would say also that I don't think (we) would rule out the possibility that one could still find those options."
Francis has run the safety board's investigation, while Kallstrom has overseen a parallel criminal investigation.
Kallstrom noted significant parts of the plane's fuselage and centre fuel tank remain missing and could contain the key to the mystery.
"Is it less likely? Well, sure. Does it mean it's not in the last 5 percent? No, it does not," he said.
"We're not saying we now think it's mechanical failure," he added. "We're just trying to talk about the realities of the situation."

Four scalloping boats have been dredging the remaining bits and pieces of the aircraft some 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) under the ocean floor, and investigators are studying an extensive mock-up of the plane's wreckage. They know the centre fuel tank exploded but have not determined why.
The remains of 215 of the 230 victims have been recovered.
